name: Vera Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays anonymous. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior carpenter on a shopfitting crew, which means we fit out the insides of shops, cafés and offices in the city centre: stud walls, counters, shelving, reception desks. A lot of it's nights, because the shop is open in the day, so I start at eight in the evening and finish at four. Lorna, our crew leader, does the drawings and the setting out, and I build what she marks. I like that it's different every week, and I hate the drive home at four in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sort of jobs are most of them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About two thirds are office fit-outs, so new meeting rooms, desks, kitchens for staff. The rest are shops and cafés. I'm not quick yet, Lorna still checks every joint on my counters, but the pay's good because of the nights. Marco, my partner, drives buses on the early shift, so we sort of pass each other in the hallway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a bit oversold. I'd probably share a funny video in the crew group chat and leave it at that. I'm not one for big arguments either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine for me. Offices still get refitted every few years, shops still change their look, and there's plenty of fit-out firms in the city if this one went quiet. What I'd actually think about is finishing my qualification, because I'm still on the junior rate for some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the crew, finish my carpentry certificate by next summer, and keep putting money aside. Marco and I bought a small flat two years ago with a low mortgage, and I've got about seven months of spending saved on top. I'd ask Lorna to let me do a bit of setting out so I learn the drawing side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Tired from the nights, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. When I've got to work out the angles on a curved counter, I'll ask the AI on my phone to check my maths before I cut. I started after Anil, the apprentice, showed me, and it saved me ruining a sheet of oak veneer. I wouldn't trust it on its own, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the job right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Speed. On a night job you've got to be out before the shop opens at nine, finished and clean. Last month I was still fixing a shelf at half eight with the manager standing behind me. Lorna stayed and helped, but I felt awful.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** and share a **funny video** in the crew chat.
I'm not one for **big arguments** either way.
think: Offices and shops still get **refitted** every few years, so work stays steady.
My real concern is finishing the **qualification** while still on the **junior rate**.
do: Finish the **carpentry certificate** by next summer.
Keep saving on top of **seven months** put aside and a low **mortgage**.
Ask Lorna, the crew leader, to teach me **setting out** from drawings.
S0.quote: When I've got to work out the angles on a curved counter, I'll ask the AI on my phone to check my maths before I cut.
fieldNote: Her work rests on **office fit-outs**, which matters for later pictures.
She uses AI **now and then**, only after a colleague showed her, which fits steady.
Main pressure is **speed** on night jobs, not money.

steps.text: Finish the carpentry certificate by next summer
Keep adding to the seven months of savings
Carry on building counters and walls on the night crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change who our customers are, and leave it there. At work I'd talk it through with Lorna, because she's seen a few booms and busts. I wouldn't be posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me more than people would guess. Two thirds of our work is fitting out offices, and if companies use AI for writing, checking and answering customers, they need fewer staff and fewer desks. Fewer desks means fewer meeting rooms to build. My hands are safe, but if companies need fewer desks, the meeting rooms I build could dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start using the AI more, for checking my angles and reading Lorna's drawings, so I'm quicker. I'd look around for fit-out firms that do more shops, cafés, and especially clinics and schools, and move if one offered. And I'd save a bit more, maybe an extra two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be watching the job list every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the office work was drying up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss would start pricing jobs lower to win them, that's the first sign. Then the nights get fewer and they let the agency lads go. I'd also look out for offices in town with whole floors to let. You can see it from the bus, Marco says, the empty floors with the lights off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco's job in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buses still need drivers in this picture, robots are slow. He'd be fine for now, I think. If anything, his steady wage is what lets me take a risk and move firms. That's what we'd say to each other.

say: I'd say AI changes **who our customers are** and leave it there.
I'd talk it through with **Lorna**, who's seen a few **booms and busts**.
think: **Two thirds** of our work is office fit-outs, and AI means **fewer desks**.
My **hands are safe**, but the jobs they do could dry up.
do: Use AI more for **angles and drawings**, so I get quicker.
Look for fit-out firms doing **clinics and schools**, and move if offered.
Save an extra **two hundred** a month.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, checking the **job list** every week.
S1.quote: My hands are safe, but if companies need fewer desks, the meeting rooms I build could dry up.
fieldNote: She sees an **indirect hit**: AI shrinks office staff, which shrinks **fit-out** demand.
Marco's **steady wage** is what lets her consider moving firms.
Her warning signs are practical: **lower prices**, fewer nights, empty floors.

steps.text: Use the phone AI to check angles and read drawings
Apply to fit-out firms working on clinics and schools
Save an extra two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, and the government needs to tell people what the plan is. I'd say it calmly, I'm not a shouter. At work I think everyone would be asking Lorna what she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, office fit-outs would stop almost overnight, because no company builds meeting rooms for staff it doesn't need. That happens in 2028, so my work drops first, three years before any robot comes for my hands. Then in 2031 the robots come for the building work and for Marco's bus. That's both of us within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast in the first year. I'd get onto a crew doing repairs and kitchens for the housing association, because people still live in houses. I'd stop the extra spending, no holiday, and keep the savings in cash. Marco and I would talk about overpaying the mortgage so it's smaller when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake after the night shift, which is saying something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why housing repairs specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a damp flat with a broken kitchen in an old block is a mess, and somebody has to sort it out on the day. My cousin Rosa works for the housing association and says the waiting list for repairs is two years long. It's not glamorous, but it's people's homes, not empty offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the three years before the robots change what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd give me time to get good at the repair work and pay down the flat. But I'd be honest with myself that 2031 is coming for that too. I'd use the three years to save and to see whether Marco wants to retrain, maybe into something with people, like the bus depot training.

say: **Nobody's ready**, and the government needs to say what the **plan** is.
I'd say it **calmly**, and everyone at work would be asking Lorna what she knows.
think: Office fit-outs would stop in **2028**, three years before robots come for my **hands**.
In **2031** robots hit building work and **Marco's bus**, so both of us go.
do: Move to a crew doing **housing repairs** and kitchens for the housing association.
Cancel the **holiday** and keep savings in **cash**.
Talk with Marco about **overpaying** the mortgage before robots arrive.
S2.quote: Office fit-outs would stop almost overnight, because no company builds meeting rooms for staff it doesn't need.
fieldNote: Her work vanishes on the **AGI date** through demand, not through robots doing her job.
She expects **both household earners** to lose work within three years.
Housing repairs is a sensible move, but she knows it only **buys time**.

steps.text: Move to a housing association repairs and kitchens crew
Cancel the holiday and keep savings in cash
Overpay the flat mortgage while both still earn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms and governments to plan, so they'd better. I'd tell people at work to get qualified while there's still time. I'd probably sound a bit like my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, office fit-outs would slow from about 2029, as companies see it coming, and stop by 2031. Robots for building come around 2034, and Marco's job about the same. So I've got three or four years of my current work and then I need to be somewhere else. It's tight, but it's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my certificate, then do a kitchen fitting course and move to housing repairs by around 2029. I'd use the AI a lot more for the drawings and quotes, because I'd want to be the one on the repair crew who can price a job. We'd overpay the mortgage every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pricing jobs is thinking work. Won't AI take that too, in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably the sums. But someone still has to stand in the flat, see the rot behind the sink and tell the tenant what's happening. I'd want to be the person who uses the AI to price the job while I'm standing there. That's my bet, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marco change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No new car, the old one's fine. We'd talk about kids, which we'd been planning for 2029, and maybe wait a year or two. That's the bit that would make me sad, if I'm honest.

say: **Five years** is enough for firms and governments to plan, so they'd better.
I'd tell people at work to get **qualified** while there's still time.
think: Office fit-outs slow around **2029**, leaving three or four years of my current work.
Robots and Marco's driverless bus come around **2034**, so I need to be **elsewhere**.
do: Finish the certificate, then take a **kitchen fitting course** and move to repairs.
Use AI more for **drawings and quotes** so I can price repair jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, but with her hands on the **wheel**.
S3.quote: Someone still has to stand in the flat, see the rot behind the sink and tell the tenant what's happening.
fieldNote: She builds a **timeline**: fit-outs fade first, then robots and buses around **2034**.
Delaying **children** is the cost she feels most.
She frames AI as a **tool for pricing** jobs on site, a steady adopter's bet.

steps.text: Take a kitchen fitting course after the certificate
Use AI to price repair jobs on site
Overpay the flat mortgage every month
Push back plans for children by a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and there's no excuse for anyone, firms, councils or people, to be caught out. I'd also say it's a good time to learn a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with ten years I'd be fine for a long while. Office fit-outs would slow in the early 2030s, robots wouldn't touch building till about 2039, and I'd be forty by then. Marco would have years to think about his next step. That feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the crew, finish the certificate, and learn kitchens and repairs on the side over a few years. I'd use AI the way the others do, for drawings and checks. We'd have kids on the plan we had, around 2029, and overpay the mortgage when we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Knowing the robots are coming in ten years is like knowing the shop will close at some point, just not this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in shopfitting the whole decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for the first few years, while the office work is still there. I'd keep an eye on how many office jobs come in each year, and when it drops, I'd move. Lorna says she'd move to retail fit-outs herself, so maybe I'd follow her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Marco to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with people in it. He's good with the older passengers, he always helps them with their bags. Maybe a job in care or at the bus station helping people. But that's his call, not mine.

say: **Ten years** is fair warning, so nobody should be **caught out**.
It's a good time to **learn a second trade**.
think: Robots won't touch building until about **2039**, when I'd be **forty**.
Marco would have **years** to think about his next step.
do: Stay on the crew and finish the **certificate**.
Learn **kitchens and repairs** on the side over a few years.
Keep the **2029 plan** for children and overpay the mortgage when possible.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **fine**, like a shop that closes someday, not this year.
S4.quote: Knowing the robots are coming in ten years is like knowing the shop will close at some point, just not this year.
fieldNote: With a decade, the **office slowdown** becomes a trend to watch rather than a cliff.
She keeps the **children** plan, which she would delay in shorter pictures.
She'd **follow Lorna**, a trusted senior, if fit-outs shifted to retail.

steps.text: Learn kitchens and repairs on the side over several years
Keep working nights on the shopfitting crew
Start a family around 2029 as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my work dries up first and then Marco's bus goes three years later. What would help is a clear list from the council of which repair and housing jobs will still need people, and paid courses for fit-out workers to move into them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. Working nights already costs a lot, you don't see your partner or your friends. If the work changes, I'd actually like a day job, so there's a small bit of good in it.

headlineQuote: If the work changes, I'd actually like a day job, so there's a small bit of good in it.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old junior shopfitter** on a night crew, still slower than she'd like.
She and Marco, a bus driver, own a **small flat** and have about **seven months** saved.
She sees that her work depends on **office fit-outs**, which shrink when AI cuts office staff.
A steady adopter, she uses AI to check her **maths** and plans a move into **housing repairs**.
She is **alarmed** in the fast picture, expecting both incomes to go, and calmer with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: her fit-out work dries up first, then Marco's **bus** goes.
whatWouldHelp: A council list of **repair jobs** that still need people, with **paid courses** to move into them.
